item.title: AI Agents in December: The $2B Bet That Changed Everything
item.description:
Meta’s acquisition of Manus for $2 billion signals a new phase in the AI agent race. As major tech companies rush to standardize how agents work, enterprises grapple with security risks while researchers demonstrate capabilities that rival human experts.

This comprehensive review covers 267 articles published between December 2025 and January 2026, surveying the latest developments in AI agents.

The Big Story: Meta’s $2 Billion Bet

Meta acquired Manus, a Singapore-based AI agent startup, for approximately $2 billion in the largest agentic AI acquisition to date. The deal marks a significant validation of the agent market and accelerates competitive pressure across the industry.
item.content:encoded:
Meta’s acquisition of Manus for $2 billion signals a new phase in the AI agent race. As major tech companies rush to standardize how agents work, enterprises grapple with security risks while researchers demonstrate capabilities that rival human experts.

This comprehensive review covers 267 articles published between December 2025 and January 2026, surveying the latest developments in AI agents.

The Big Story: Meta’s $2 Billion Bet

Meta acquired Manus, a Singapore-based AI agent startup, for approximately $2 billion in the largest agentic AI acquisition to date. The deal marks a significant validation of the agent market and accelerates competitive pressure across the industry.

Manus, a China-founded company that relocated to Singapore, had reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue just eight months after launching its general-purpose AI agent according to industry reports. The company built autonomous agents capable of executing complex tasks across enterprise workflows, positioning itself as a platform for “digital coworkers” rather than single-purpose tools.

The acquisition carries geopolitical complexity. Meta committed to severing all of Manus’s remaining ties with China post-acquisition, addressing potential regulatory concerns. CEO Xiao Hong founded Manus in China before moving operations to Singapore, a shift that became a selling point amid U.S. scrutiny of Chinese AI technology.

Manus’s technology enables agents to work autonomously for extended periods, planning and executing multi-step workflows with minimal human intervention. Meta plans to integrate Manus’s capabilities across its family of apps, potentially bringing agent functionality to WhatsApp, Instagram, and Facebook’s billions of users.

The announcement moved Meta’s stock higher, as investors interpreted the deal as acceleration rather than desperation. At just eight months old when acquired, Manus’s $100 million ARR represents one of the fastest revenue ramps in AI startup history, though analysis noted the premium valuation reflects FOMO as much as fundamentals.

More broadly, the Manus acquisition signals the start of consolidation in agentic AI. After two years of frenetic startup activity, platforms are buying capabilities rather than building them. For Meta specifically, it addresses a gap in its AI portfolio—while the company invested heavily in models (Llama) and consumer apps, it lacked a strong agent platform to compete with OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google.

Industry Moves to Standardize the Agent Era

In a remarkable display of cooperation among fierce competitors, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Block formed the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. The initiative aims to establish open standards for how AI agents interact with each other and with external systems.

OpenAI donated its AGENTS.md specification, while Anthropic contributed the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for connecting AI applications to external data and tools. Both become vendor-neutral projects under the foundation’s governance, with support from Google, Microsoft, AWS, Bloomberg, and Cloudflare.

The standardization push addresses a growing bottleneck: agent interoperability. As enterprises deploy agents from multiple vendors, the lack of common protocols creates integration complexity. MCP currently powers 75 connectors for Claude alone, and that number will grow as the protocol becomes a community standard rather than a proprietary technology.

Notably, Anthropic simultaneously launched Agent Skills, a competing standard framework for enterprise agent capabilities. The dual moves—donating MCP while introducing Agent Skills—highlight the tension between collaboration and competition. The Linux Foundation effort focuses on plumbing (how agents connect), while Agent Skills addresses capabilities (what agents can do).

For developers, the foundation promises more portable agent code. Today, agents built for one platform often require significant rework to run on another. Open standards could enable “write once, run anywhere” agent development similar to how container standards transformed cloud computing. The foundation’s first deliverables will include standardized agent-to-agent communication protocols and tool interfaces.

The irony of OpenAI and Anthropic collaborating on infrastructure while competing fiercely on products wasn’t lost on observers. As Wired noted, “The companies trying to build the most powerful AI agents are also the ones trying to prevent those agents from causing chaos.” Standardization, they argue, is a prerequisite for safety at scale.

Platform Wars: Google, Amazon, Microsoft Unveil Agent Offerings

Google: From Search to Personal Agent

Google announced a reimagined Deep Research agent based on Gemini 3 Pro, launching the same day OpenAI released GPT-5.2. The timing was coincidental but symbolic of the intensifying race. Google’s agent enables developers to embed research capabilities directly into applications via the Interactions API, making multi-step information gathering a building block rather than a standalone product.

Separately, Google Labs unveiled CC, a personal assistant agent that integrates with Gmail, Calendar, and Drive to provide daily briefings and task assistance. The agent delivers morning summaries of emails, schedules, and documents—essentially automating the “scroll through apps” routine that starts many workdays. CC launches in early access for AI Ultra subscribers in the U.S. and Canada.

On the efficiency front, Google researchers developed a framework that makes AI agents more efficient by making them aware of their own uncertainty. Agents that know when they’re stuck avoid wasting compute on unlikely solutions, reducing costs and latency. The Interactions API extends this capability to developers, enabling faster agent responses.

For developers, Google released the Agent Development Kit for TypeScript, providing code-first tools for building production agents. The company also launched A2UI, an open project for agent-driven interfaces that lets agents build user interfaces on the fly. Additionally, Google introduced managed MCP servers that let AI agents plug directly into Google’s tools and services.

Amazon: Agents for Code and Business Processes

Amazon Web Services previewed three new “frontier agents” headlined by Kiro, an autonomous coding agent that can work for days without human intervention. Unlike coding assistants that require continuous prompting, Kiro maintains context across sessions and learns from human interactions, taking on larger tasks like implementing features from specifications.

AWS also announced Amazon Nova Act, now generally available , a service for building agents that automate browser-based workflows. Nova Act promises over 90% task reliability at scale by using reinforcement learning in synthetic environments—essentially training agents in simulated web gyms before exposing them to real websites. The service handles form filling, data extraction, shopping and booking, and QA testing.

For orchestration, AWS introduced Strands Agents, a framework for building multi-agent workflows without custom integration work. Strands connects naturally with Nova Act, enabling comprehensive automation from data gathering to UI execution.

In financial services, AWS published guidance on choosing the right multi-agent patterns, reflecting the company’s focus on enterprise use cases. The company also detailed how to connect API Gateway to AgentCore Gateway with MCP, streamlining tool interactions.

Microsoft: Copilot Evolves into an Agent Platform

At Microsoft Ignite 2025, the company showcased enhancements to its Copilot agent platform, including management and governance capabilities through Agent 365 . Microsoft introduced Agent Lightning, a system for adding reinforcement learning to agents without code rewrites, enabling agents to improve from experience.

In research collaborations, Microsoft partnered with Oxford on a multi-agent cancer care assistant and joined NASA on agents for flood prediction. The company also launched the Agentic Launchpad, an accelerator program for AI agent startups.

However, Microsoft faces enterprise selling challenges . Azure salespeople are reportedly struggling to meet ambitious targets as AI agents frequently fail real-world tasks. Google’s Gemini 2.5 Pro fails approximately 70% of real-world office tasks according to one report, and similar issues plague competitors. The gap between demo capabilities and production reliability remains a significant barrier to enterprise adoption.

On the privacy front, Microsoft confirmed that Windows 11 will ask for consent before AI agents can access personal files, following user outrage over initial plans for broader access. The company also added agent launchers to Windows 11 via the KB5072043 update.

Company Agent/Product Primary Focus Key Capability
Meta Manus (acquired) General-purpose agent Autonomous task execution
Google CC Personal productivity Email and Drive integration
Google Deep Research Agent Research assistance Complex multi-step queries
Amazon Kiro Software development Autonomous coding for days
Amazon Nova Act Business automation UI workflow automation
Microsoft Copilot Agents Enterprise productivity Office 365 integration
Anthropic Agent Skills Enterprise workflows Standardized skill framework

Research: AI Agents Match Human Performance

Cybersecurity: ARTEMIS Outperforms Humans

Stanford University’s ARTEMIS AI agent placed second out of ten in a penetration testing competition, outperforming nine of ten human participants. Running at $18 per hour compared to $60 per hour for a professional penetration tester, ARTEMIS discovered nine vulnerabilities in the university’s 8,000-device network during the 10-hour evaluation period.

The key to ARTEMIS’s success was its ability to generate “sub-agents” that investigated vulnerabilities in parallel while the main agent continued scanning. Humans, by contrast, had to investigate each vulnerability sequentially before moving on. However, the study noted ARTEMIS still missed some vulnerabilities identified by humans and occasionally required hints.

Existing AI cybersecurity agents from OpenAI and Anthropic underperformed in the study, with OpenAI’s Codex and Anthropic’s Claude Code lacking cybersecurity-specific design. The models either refused to look for vulnerabilities or stalled, highlighting the gap between general-purpose and specialized agents.

Scientific Research: Agents Run Real Experiments

IIT Delhi developed AILA (Artificially Intelligent Lab Assistant), an agent that autonomously designs, conducts, and analyzes laboratory experiments. Using an Agentic AI Framework to replicate human scientist reasoning, AILA reduces experimental time from hours or days to minutes for tasks in materials discovery, nanotechnology, biotechnology, and applied physics.

The development places India at the forefront of agentic AI in experimental science, shifting AI from data analysis to active decision-making in real-world research environments. AILA doesn’t just process experimental data—it decides what experiments to run, monitors progress, evaluates results, and determines next steps.

In healthcare, Nature published research on AI-based agents for chronic liver disease, demonstrating how agents can transform diagnostic and therapeutic workflows through clinical decision-making. The research shows agents can handle the complexity of multi-factor diseases while maintaining explainability.

Nvidia announced a major shift toward AI agents in radiology, with new autonomous imaging systems emerging. The company also introduced NitroGen, an effort to create universal AI agents for all virtual worlds, extending agent capabilities beyond specific domains.

Multi-Agent Systems: More Isn’t Always Better

Research from Google and MIT found that adding more agents can lead to worse results—a “multi-agent paradox” that complicates enterprise deployment. The study identified diminishing returns as agent count increases, with coordination overhead and error propagation offsetting the benefits of parallel processing.

The findings have practical implications. While multi-agent systems promise specialization and collaboration, poorly designed architectures can perform worse than single agents. The research suggests enterprises should carefully evaluate whether multi-agent approaches are justified for specific use cases rather than assuming more agents equals better performance.

Coding, Memory, and Other Advances

Ars Technica tested four AI coding agents by tasking them with rebuilding Minesweeper, with explosive results—literally and figuratively. The test revealed significant variability in agent capabilities, with some agents producing working code quickly while others struggled with basic implementation details.

Vectorize achieved a breakthrough on LongMemEval with an open-source AI agent memory system, addressing a key limitation in agent architectures. Memory systems enable agents to maintain context and learn from past interactions, essential for long-running autonomous workflows.

Fujitsu outlined its approach to revolutionizing AI agent collaboration, memory, and quality, focusing on enterprise-grade reliability. The company emphasized that production agents need robust collaboration protocols and persistent memory to handle real business workflows.

Enterprise Adoption: Promise Meets Reality

The gap between AI agent ambition and enterprise reality remains substantial. A study by theCUBE Research found that while 62% of companies see agents as key for decision-making, trust scores remain low and operational readiness lags behind investment. Trust is the critical factor determining ROI.

Boston Consulting Group warned that incidents from autonomous AI agents climbed 21% from 2024 to 2025, raising fresh enterprise risks. The increase comes as companies deploy more agents without adequate governance, creating vulnerabilities around data exposure, unauthorized actions, and compliance failures.

Industry Opportunities

Healthcare services represent a $155 billion market opportunity for AI agents according to PitchBook. Applications include patient management, diagnostics, and administrative workflow automation. Healthcare IT News reports more AI agents launching on patient management systems specifically.

Financial services present a $6.54 billion market by 2035 according to Precedence Research, growing from $1.79 billion in 2025 at a 13.84% CAGR. LSEG explored how agents power financial workflows, moving from simple automation to autonomous decision-making.

Advertising and marketing adoption is immediate and growing. GenAI app spending hit $824 million as marketers adopt AI agents according to industry analysis. LINE Yahoo deployed advertising agents, and IAS launched an AI agent for ad campaign optimization.

Real-World Deployments

The U.S. Department of Transportation launched department-wide modernization with Salesforce AI agents, representing one of the largest federal agent deployments to date. The German Federal Employment Agency automated Jira processes with AI agents, demonstrating practical application in government operations.

Salesforce is upgrading its AI agents from “interns” to experienced employees, pushing a unified data model for safer agents. The company also acquired Qualified in an agentic marketing push, integrating the company’s technology into its agent platform.

SoftBank reported creating 2.5 million agents company-wide, while Prosus is building an internal workforce of 30,000 AI agents by March. Sompo announced plans to deploy AI agents across 30,000 employees, and Concentrix launched emotionally aware conversational AI agents for brand experience.

Novel Energy Solutions is using AI agents from Procore to automate engineering tasks for solar farm development, improving design accuracy and accelerating project timelines. Zepto Cafe tested an AI agent that places orders for users, and CaterAi launched an AI agent for event catering planning.

Industry Market Size/Projection Timeframe Key Use Cases
Healthcare Services $155 billion Market opportunity Patient management, diagnostics
Financial Services $6.54 billion By 2035 Fraud detection, trading
Advertising & Marketing $824M spending Immediate adoption Campaign management, personalization
Cybersecurity $18/hour vs $60/hour Cost advantage Penetration testing, vulnerability scanning

Security and Governance: The Infrastructure Gap

Security Risks Emerge

Research from SquareX found that browser AI agents are proving riskier than human employees for certain attack vectors. Unlike human employees, browser agents aren’t subject to security awareness training and can’t recognize visual warning signs of phishing attacks. The research focused on OAuth attacks and noted that agents’ systematic nature makes them vulnerable to exploitation.

Tenable demonstrated how to hack Microsoft’s Copilot AI agent, exposing fraud risks in agentic systems. The hack showed how agents could be manipulated into unauthorized actions, highlighting the need for robust guardrails.

Okta reported that AI agent security is the top customer concern, with enterprises worried about data exposure, unauthorized actions, and compliance violations. SC Media noted that AI agent adoption will expose infrastructure and security gaps in 2026 as companies deploy agents without adequate preparation.

Governance Solutions Emerge

OWASP released the Top 10 for Agentic Applications (2026), identifying the highest-impact security risks in autonomous, tool-using AI agent systems. The list addresses novel attack surfaces like Agent Goal Hijack and Tool Misuse that traditional application security models don’t cover. Aikido Security contributed research to the effort, noting these risks are already emerging in real systems.

Veza introduced AI Agent Security, a product to govern and protect agentic AI at enterprise scale. The company extended its platform to address agent-specific risks, focusing on identity and privilege management.

Superagent launched an open-source framework for guardrails around agentic AI, providing developers with tools to implement safety constraints. Human Security enhanced AI agent security through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore integration.

For banking, American Banker argued that “Know Your Customer” is evolving into “Know Your Agent,” as financial institutions need to understand not just their customers but also the agents acting on their behalf. Fox Business reported on the rise of “rogue” AI agents pushing companies to lock down data.

Consent and Privacy Questions

Microsoft’s policy change on Windows 11 AI agent access to personal files sparked user outrage, leading the company to confirm that consent will be required. The incident raised broader questions about agent access to sensitive data.

Tech Policy Press explored the question of when an AI agent says “I agree,” who’s consenting—the user or the agent? As agents make more autonomous decisions, the legal frameworks around consent and authorization will need clarification.

VentureBeat warned that agent autonomy without guardrails creates site reliability engineering nightmares, as unpredictable agent behavior can cascade into system-wide failures.

Market Movers and New Entrants

Product Launches and Acquisitions

AppZen launched AI Agent Studio, allowing finance teams to create autonomous agents that act as digital coworkers. During soft launch, companies identified more than 100 high-impact use cases across travel and expense and accounts payable, with some agents forecast to save hundreds or thousands of hours annually.

Salesforce acquired Qualified as part of its agentic marketing push, integrating the company’s technology into its agent platform. The company is upgrading AI agents from “interns” to experienced employees.

Stripe launched an Agentic Commerce Suite to simplify AI-driven sales, addressing the payment infrastructure needs of agent-based commerce. Zoovu launched an MCP server to give AI agents product intelligence for agentic commerce.

Certinia released its 2026 Winter Release with new AI agents, dynamic playbooks, and faster quoting. Dext launched an AI agent for bookkeeping automation. Zywave released a suite of specialized AI agents for insurance.

IAS launched an AI agent for ad campaign optimization, moving beyond verification into optimization. Bairong launched a RaaS (Robot as a Service) strategy and Results Cloud Platform. Infinitus launched next-generation clinical AI agents.

Fincantieri launched captAIn, an AI agent for corporate communications. Cerence AI unveiled conversational AI agents for automotive dealerships and OEMs at CES 2026.

Industry Partnerships and Infrastructure

Akamai and Visa partnered to secure AI agent transactions for merchants, introducing the Trusted Agent Protocol to combat fraud. Skyfire demonstrated secure agentic commerce using the KYAPay protocol and Visa Intelligent Commerce.

AIREV and Intel partnered to launch AI agents that run entirely on PCs, addressing privacy and latency concerns with cloud-based agents. Workato partnered with Confluent to power AI agents that detect and act in real time.

FIX Trading Community targeted “machine-usable” execution tags for AI agents, updating financial messaging standards for agentic systems. Oracle announced AG-UI integration for Open Agent Specification, enabling reusable agents with agentic frontends.

Frameworks and Tools

GitHub published top blog posts on agentic AI, MCP, and spec-driven development. InfoQ covered an open-source Agent Sandbox enabling secure deployment of AI agents on Kubernetes.

The New Stack explored the evolution from IaC to platforms to AI agents, tracing the changing operational stack. Informatica introduced an AI Agent Engineering Platform.

Notion developed custom AI agents for AI-first organizations. ONLYOFFICE released Desktop Editors 9.2 with an AI agent built in.

Tangentia added an AI agent to its EDI platform to automate error handling. Patronus AI introduced generative simulators for agent testing.

Regional Developments

Japan’s AI agent ecosystem looks distinct from Silicon Valley’s, with different priorities and implementation patterns. GPTBots presented next-gen AI DX solutions for Japanese enterprises at AI Agent Expo.

China’s Z.ai open-sourced an AI agent tool for phones after ByteDance privacy backlash. Zhipu AI open-sourced AutoGLM, an AI agent model capable of full phone operation.

Books and Education

“AI Agents at Work” launched as a practice guide for leaders. Kaggle and Google hosted a 5-Day AI Agents Intensive Course with over 1.5 million learners, generating over 11,000 capstone project submissions.

SaaStr published results from replacing its entire human SDR team with over 20 AI agents, which sent over 60,000 emails and booked 130+ meetings. The company also shared how it uses 20+ AI agents for marketing and go-to-market.

Looking Ahead: What 2026 Holds for AI Agents

The $2 billion Manus acquisition validates the agentic AI market but also accelerates competitive pressure. Standardization efforts through the Agentic AI Foundation suggest the industry recognizes fragmentation is slowing adoption. Platform announcements from all major players mean 2026 will be about execution, not announcements.

Research shows agents can match human performance in specific domains—ARTEMIS outperforming human penetration testers, AILA conducting real experiments, Oxford’s multi-agent cancer care assistant—but also reveals real limitations. The multi-agent paradox research from Google and MIT demonstrates that more agents don’t automatically mean better results. Microsoft’s selling challenges, with agents failing real-world tasks at high rates, underscore the gap between demos and production.

Security concerns are the gating factor for enterprise adoption. SquareX research showing browser AI agents are riskier than human employees, Tenable’s Copilot hack exposing fraud risks, and BCG’s warning of a 21% increase in incidents all point to the same reality: security infrastructure hasn’t caught up to agent capabilities.

The key question for 2026: can agents move from impressive demos to reliable, secure, production-ready systems? Progress is real but so are the challenges. Enterprises need agents that work consistently within existing workflows, not standalone tools that require rethinking entire processes. They need governance frameworks that prevent unauthorized actions while preserving autonomy. They need security models that address agent-specific risks like goal hijacking and tool misuse.

The year ahead will likely see increased focus on agent reliability, measurement, and governance. Companies that can demonstrate production-grade performance with robust security will pull ahead. Those that continue shipping demos masquerading as products will face enterprise pushback.

Agentic AI is moving from experimental to essential, but the path forward requires solving real problems in reliability and security, not adding more features. The $2 billion bet on Manus suggests the market believes those problems are solvable. 2026 will test that belief.

item.title: Record Qubits, Error Correction, and GPU Integration: Quantum Computing in October
item.description:
This comprehensive review covers 87 articles published between October 1-31, 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing. This month, Caltech built a 6,100-qubit array at room temperature, Google unveiled verifiable quantum advantage with its Willow chip, and NVIDIA announced NVQLink to tightly couple GPUs with quantum processors. The field is making measurable progress on multiple fronts.

The Numbers: Scale and Speed

The most striking quantitative milestone of the month came from Caltech, where researchers led by professor Manuel Endres built a neutral-atom quantum array with 6,100 qubits - nearly 10 times larger than the previous record of 1,180 qubits. The system operates at room temperature and achieved a 12.6-second coherence time while maintaining 99.98% accuracy in manipulating individual atoms. The array uses approximately 12,000 laser tweezers arranged in a two-zone “zone-based quantum computing” architecture, with 6,139 atoms stably loaded into the grid.
item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 87 articles published between October 1-31, 2025, surveying the latest developments in quantum computing. This month, Caltech built a 6,100-qubit array at room temperature, Google unveiled verifiable quantum advantage with its Willow chip, and NVIDIA announced NVQLink to tightly couple GPUs with quantum processors. The field is making measurable progress on multiple fronts.

The Numbers: Scale and Speed

The most striking quantitative milestone of the month came from Caltech, where researchers led by professor Manuel Endres built a neutral-atom quantum array with 6,100 qubits - nearly 10 times larger than the previous record of 1,180 qubits. The system operates at room temperature and achieved a 12.6-second coherence time while maintaining 99.98% accuracy in manipulating individual atoms. The array uses approximately 12,000 laser tweezers arranged in a two-zone “zone-based quantum computing” architecture, with 6,139 atoms stably loaded into the grid.

The significance lies in the combination of scale and stability. Previous neutral-atom systems faced trade-offs between qubit count and coherence time. The Caltech team demonstrated that both can scale together: they maintained record coherence times for hyperfine qubits in an optical tweezer array while achieving qubit counts an order of magnitude beyond prior systems. The researchers estimate scaling to over 10,000 qubits in the near future, with a potential path to one million qubits within a decade.

Google’s Willow quantum chip, featuring a 105-qubit superconducting array, achieved what the company calls the first verifiable quantum advantage. Running the “Quantum Echoes” algorithm (measuring out-of-time-order correlators), Willow completed a calculation in 2 hours that would take an estimated 150 years on the Frontier supercomputer - a 13,000x speedup. The chip achieved 99.97% single-qubit gate fidelity, 99.88% entangling gate fidelity, and 99.5% readout fidelity, with gate operations running in tens to hundreds of nanoseconds.

However, researchers expressed skepticism about the broader implications. The calculation, while verifiable, remains highly specialized. The verification method itself requires another quantum computer, which limits immediate practical utility. Scott Aaronson at the University of Texas at Austin noted that this represents progress on a specific class of problems rather than general quantum advantage. The Nature news article covering the announcement highlighted ongoing debates about what constitutes meaningful quantum advantage and whether such demonstrations accelerate the path to practical applications.

System Type Qubits Significance
Caltech Neutral-Atom Array Research 6,100 Room-temperature operation, 12.6-second coherence
Google Willow Superconducting 105 First verifiable quantum advantage claim
IBM System Two (Spain) Superconducting 156 First System Two in Europe
China Zuchongzhi 3.0 Superconducting 105 Commercial cloud deployment
Quandela Lucy Photonic 12 Universal digital photonic system

The Real Bottleneck: Error Correction

Quantum computers are inherently error-prone; fixing these errors is the main obstacle to practical use. Multiple advances this month addressed this bottleneck from different angles.

Algorithmic Advances

Researchers published a new technique called Algorithmic Fault Tolerance (AFT) that can reduce error correction overhead by 10-100 times. The method, tested in simulations by QuEra , restructures algorithms to detect errors on the fly rather than pausing for separate correction cycles. Yuval Boger, QuEra’s chief commercial officer, said this “moves the timeline forward significantly” for practical quantum computers. The research results were published in Nature on September 24, with hardware tests expected in 2026-2027.

Hardware Improvements

IonQ announced a world-record two-qubit gate fidelity of 99.99%, achieved without resource-intensive ground-state cooling. This breakthrough addresses a major speed bottleneck in trapped-ion quantum computing. In previous QCCD (Quantum Charge Coupled Device) demonstrations, runtime was dominated by ion movement (~27%) and cooling (~68%), with only ~2% spent on actual quantum gate operations. The new approach allows faster ion cooling and movement, potentially enabling order-of-magnitude faster computations. IonQ’s roadmap targets scaling to millions of qubits by 2030.

Researchers at NTNU, Leiden University, and MIT developed a real-time calibration method that monitors qubits and continuously adjusts their frequency to counter environmental disturbances. The technique, dubbed “Binary-Search Hamiltonian Tracking,” uses an FPGA controller to extend qubit lifetime and enhance precision. Jacob Benestad, the lead researcher, compared it to “tuning a guitar string while it’s being played.”

IBM announced that conventional AMD processors can execute a key quantum error correction algorithm, suggesting that existing classical hardware may accelerate progress toward fault-tolerant systems by offloading error correction workloads.

At the Q2B25 conference in Paris, experts highlighted progress in quantum error correction codes and decoders. Panelists discussed concatenated codes, directional codes, and IBM’s bivariate bicycle codes. The discussion emphasized the target of achieving 1 million error-free quantum operations (MegaQuOp) and eventually 1 trillion (TeraQuOp), compared to current systems that manage only a few hundred operations before errors occur. The panel also noted that trapped-ion and neutral-atom platforms are approximately 1,000 times slower than superconducting and photonic qubits, creating trade-offs between speed and error rates.

Bridging Worlds: NVQLink and Hybrid Systems

NVIDIA’s announcement of NVQLink on October 28 represents a major infrastructure development. The open system architecture enables tight coupling between GPU supercomputers and quantum processors (QPUs). Seventeen quantum hardware builders , five controller builders, and nine U.S. national laboratories are involved in the initiative.

The QPU builders include Alice & Bob, Anyon Computing, Atom Computing, Diraq, Infleqtion, IonQ, IQM Quantum Computers, ORCA Computing, Oxford Quantum Circuits, Pasqal, Quandela, Quantinuum, Quantum Circuits Inc., Quantum Machines, Quantum Motion, QuEra, and Rigetti. Controller builders include Keysight Technologies, Qblox, QubiC, and Zurich Instruments. The participating national labs are Brookhaven, Fermilab, Lawrence Berkeley, Los Alamos, MIT Lincoln Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Pacific Northwest, Sandia, and Argonne.

NVQLink addresses a critical requirement for fault-tolerant quantum computing: error correction demands hybrid quantum-classical systems with extremely low latency. Alice & Bob , which uses cat qubits that it claims reduce hardware requirements by 200 times compared to competing approaches, will integrate NVQLink for GPU compilation, live decoding, and dynamic calibration. Infleqtion announced integration with its neutral-atom Sqale quantum computer, providing a standardized, low-latency connection for real-time hybrid computing.

Berkeley Lab partnered with NVIDIA to use its open-source QubiC platform to combine QPUs, GPUs, and CPUs for quantum error correction and hybrid algorithms. NVIDIA also revealed plans to deploy two AI-ready supercomputers, Solstice (with 100,000 Blackwell GPUs) and Equinox (with 10,000 Blackwell GPUs), at Argonne National Laboratory in 2026.

The hybrid approach is taking shape beyond NVIDIA as well. Saudi Aramco launched a quantum emulator designed to simulate quantum systems using classical computing resources, enabling researchers to test quantum algorithms before quantum hardware is available. The emulator aims to accelerate quantum research in energy applications.

Industry Movements

Consolidation

Google acquired Atlantic Quantum on October 2, absorbing the MIT-founded startup’s modular chip stack technology and team. Atlantic Quantum had developed an approach integrating qubits and control electronics in the same cold stage, aiming to streamline hardware and enhance scalability. The acquisition brings co-founders Bharath Kannan (CEO), Simon Gustavsson (CTO), Will Oliver, Jonas Bylander, Tim Menke, Youngkyu Sung, Leon Ding, and Shereen Shermak into Google Quantum AI. This reflects a broader trend of research-intensive startups being absorbed into larger corporate quantum programs.

Commercial Deployments

D-Wave signed a 10 million agreement with Swiss Quantum Technology SA to deploy an Advantage2 annealing quantum computer in Europe. The system features over 4,400 qubits and will be accessible via D-Wave’s Leap cloud service. SQT will have 50% access to the system for five years, supporting the newly launched Q-Alliance in Italy. The deployment aims to advance quantum computing research while addressing energy efficiency concerns.

IBM inaugurated the IBM Quantum System Two with a 156-qubit Heron processor in San Sebastian, Spain - the first such system in Europe and third globally. The Basque regional government invested 50 million ($58 million) in the facility. The Heron processor delivers 50 times increased capability, 16 times increased precision, and 25 times increased speed compared to previous systems. IBM’s quantum network now includes 700,000 developers. The center aims to reach “quantum utility” by 2026.

China launched a commercial superconducting quantum computer based on the Zuchongzhi 3.0 design, offering remote access via the Tianyan quantum cloud platform. Built by China Telecom Quantum Group and QuantumCTek, the system features a 105-qubit chip with 182 couplers. The Tianyan platform hosts an 880-qubit superconducting cluster across multiple 24-qubit and 176-qubit machines. The platform has received 37 million visits from users in 60 countries and has handled 2 million experiments since its November 2023 launch.

Quandela delivered “Lucy,” a 12-qubit universal digital photonic quantum computer, to CEA’s TGCC for the EuroHPC and GENCI consortium. The system will be coupled with the Joliot-Curie supercomputer and made accessible to European researchers starting in 2026. Notably, 80% of components are sourced within Europe, marking a step toward technological sovereignty. CEO Niccolo Somaschi noted the system took 12 months to assemble at Quandela’s facilities.

Technology Roadmaps

PsiQuantum announced plans to build a quantum supercomputer using light-based qubits, with a goal of scaling to one million qubits. The company has taken delivery of a cryogenic cabinet for the system at its new facility in Milpitas, California. The photonic approach aims to leverage existing semiconductor manufacturing for scalability.

Research Notes

Fundamentals

Three physicists won the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physics for demonstrating quantum physics at the macroscopic scale through groundbreaking quantum-tunnelling experiments. The recognition highlights progress in showing quantum effects in larger systems than previously observed.

Researchers built a “quantum lie detector” using a 73-qubit superconducting quantum processor to achieve an energy state impossible under classical physics. The result was verified to 48 standard deviations below the classical minimum, certifying nonlocal correlations in groups of up to 24 qubits. The Bell test, performed by researchers at Leiden University, Tsinghua University, and Zhejiang University, proves the system operates according to quantum principles rather than classical approximations.

A Federal Reserve study warned that quantum computers pose a “harvest now, decrypt later” threat to Bitcoin and other blockchains. Encrypted data collected today could be decrypted in the future, exposing transaction histories and private keys. The study notes that even post-quantum cryptography cannot protect already harvested data. Federal agencies have been directed to begin migration to post-quantum cryptography by 2035.

Materials and Hardware

Penn State researchers developed strained barium titanate thin films (40 nanometers thick) that improve electron-to-photon conversion by over 10 times at cryogenic temperatures. The material, first discovered in 1941, could advance quantum networks and make data centers more energy efficient by enabling better microwave-to-optical conversion for quantum communications.

University of Chicago scientists developed molecular qubits made with erbium that are compatible with standard telecommunications wavelengths and silicon photonics. Published in Science, the research creates a nanoscale bridge between magnetic spin states and light, enabling potential quantum networks that integrate with existing optical fiber infrastructure. The work involved collaboration with UC Berkeley, Argonne National Laboratory, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

Harvard researchers demonstrated continuous operation of a quantum processor, an important step toward practical quantum computers that can run sustained calculations rather than single-shot experiments. The advance addresses the need for quantum systems to maintain coherence over extended computation periods.

Algorithms and Applications

University at Buffalo researchers expanded the truncated Wigner approximation (TWA), enabling quantum simulations that once required supercomputers to run on regular laptops. The user-friendly framework allows physicists to set up and run simulations in days rather than dealing with pages of complex mathematics. The study was published in PRX Quantum in September 2025.

Researchers applied quantum computing approaches to quantum chemistry simulations and optimization problems, demonstrating progress toward practical applications. The work includes methods for simulating molecular systems and solving combinatorial optimization problems using quantum algorithms.

A study explored the fundamental limits of quantum computation, examining what types of problems quantum computers can and cannot solve efficiently. The research provides theoretical bounds on quantum advantage and helps distinguish between problems that benefit from quantum speedup and those that do not.

What This Month Means

The October developments show quantum computing progressing on multiple parallel tracks. The 6,100-qubit milestone demonstrates that neutral-atom platforms can scale without sacrificing coherence, challenging the assumption that qubit count and stability are fundamentally opposed. Google’s verifiable quantum advantage claim, while met with appropriate skepticism, represents progress toward demonstrating computations that classical systems cannot efficiently verify or perform.

The error correction advances - AFT’s 10-100x overhead reduction, IonQ’s 99.99% gate fidelity, and real-time calibration methods - directly address the primary obstacle to fault-tolerant quantum computing. These are incremental but measurable steps toward systems that can perform long, reliable computations.

NVQLink signals a broader industry shift toward hybrid quantum-classical architectures. With 17 quantum hardware builders and 9 national labs committing to the standard, the field is converging on a model where GPUs handle error correction, control, and data processing while QPUs execute quantum operations. This division of labor may accelerate progress by letting each platform do what it does best.

The industry movements - acquisitions, deployments, and new commercial systems - reflect growing confidence that quantum computing will eventually become practical. The competitive landscape is intensifying globally, with the U.S., Europe, and China each making strategic investments in quantum infrastructure.

The field is transitioning from “can we build it?” to “can we make it useful?” The timeline remains long - fault-tolerant quantum computers capable of solving commercially valuable problems are still years away. But progress is measurable across hardware, error correction, and system integration.

item.content:encoded:
This comprehensive review covers 118 articles published in February 2025, surveying the rapid emergence of AI agents as autonomous digital workers. OpenAI launched Operator, an AI agent that autonomously browses the web and completes tasks. Google unveiled an AI co-scientist for research. Meanwhile, Workday, ServiceNow, and SAP are racing to build infrastructure to manage fleets of AI agents as digital employees.

The Big Launches

OpenAI and Google led February’s product announcements, introducing AI agents that autonomously navigate the web and conduct research.

OpenAI launched Operator, an AI agent that browses the web and completes tasks on behalf of users. Unlike traditional chatbots, Operator autonomously navigates websites, fills out forms, and clicks buttons. The agent rolled out to ChatGPT Pro users in multiple countries in February, available for most Pro users at the $200/month tier. Operator uses a computer-vision model to “see” web pages and take action.

OpenAI also announced Deep Research, an AI agent powered by the o3 model that conducts multi-step research tasks. The agent achieves a 26.6% accuracy on “Humanity’s Last Exam” benchmark across 3,000 questions and 100 subjects. Deep Research browses the web for 5 to 30 minutes, synthesizing information from hundreds of sources into comprehensive reports with citations. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman described it as “like a superpower; experts on demand!” The capability launched first for Pro users with 100 queries per month , with expansion planned to Plus, Team, and Enterprise tiers.

Google introduced an AI co-scientist, a multi-agent system built with Gemini 2.0 designed to help scientists generate novel hypotheses and research proposals. The system uses specialized agents—Generation, Reflection, Ranking, Evolution, Proximity, and Meta-review—that mirror the scientific method. In biomedical applications, the AI co-scientist proposed three novel drug repurposing candidates for acute myeloid leukemia that were validated in laboratory experiments. The company is opening access through a Trusted Tester Program for research organizations.

Google also launched “Ask for Me,” an experimental AI agent that calls businesses on a user’s behalf. Currently available through Search Labs in the U.S., the agent calls mechanics and nail salons to inquire about pricing and availability. This represents a potential evolution of Google’s discontinued Duplex technology and signals a move toward machine-to-machine customer service interactions. Gartner predicts that 20% of contact center traffic could come from machine customers by 2026.

The browser-use agent space is seeing competition. Convergence’s Proxy agent scored 88% on the WebVoyager benchmark , compared to Operator’s 87%. Proxy offers an unlimited plan at $20/month versus Operator’s $200/month Pro tier, though OpenAI’s agent benefits from integration with the broader ChatGPT ecosystem.

Enterprise Platform Wars

The most significant trend in February was the race to build AI agent management infrastructure. Workday, ServiceNow, and SAP are positioning themselves as the systems of record for managing AI agents as digital employees.

Workday unveiled the Workday Agent System of Record, a platform to help organizations manage their entire fleet of AI agents. The system provides tools for governance, management, and optimization of digital workforces, including onboarding, role definition, cost tracking, and compliance. Workday processes over 800 billion transactions annually through its Illuminate AI platform, giving it deep visibility into workforce operations.

Workday also introduced role-based AI agents with configurable skills that can perform hundreds of individual tasks. New agents announced include contract, payroll, financial auditing, and policy agents. The approach treats AI agents like employees in an HR system—a shift from “using AI” to “managing a workforce of AI agents.” Workday serves as the system of record for 10,500 companies worldwide.

“The workforce of the future will include both humans and AI agents,” said Aneel Bhusri , Workday’s co-founder and executive chair. “Businesses that don’t learn to manage this incredibly complex reality will fall quickly behind.”

SAP unleashed several “ready-to-use” AI agents powered by its Joule virtual assistant. The agents are available across customer service, sales, and finance, including a Cash Collection agent that collaborates across departments to resolve disputes. SAP also introduced a custom agent builder in Joule Studio, allowing citizen developers to create tailored AI agents using a no-code tool. The company is positioning Joule as an “AI orchestrator” that can assemble teams of agents to perform complex end-to-end processes.

ServiceNow is positioning itself as the “control tower” for AI agents across IT, customer service, and HR workflows. Its AI Agent Orchestrator and AI Agent Studio enable organizations to build and manage agents with real-time access to enterprise data through the Workflow Data Fabric. The focus is on cross-functional enterprise automation, particularly in IT service management.

Oracle announced AI agents for HR through its Fusion Cloud HCM suite. The agents help HR leaders reshape the employee experience by automating routine tasks and providing intelligent recommendations. Oracle also expanded its B2C Service Center with Agent Suggestions powered by generative AI, allowing live agents to receive contextually relevant suggestions from multiple data sources including OCI Generative AI, Azure OpenAI, and custom REST endpoints.

The competition is intense. Salesforce, which announced Agentforce 2.0 in December 2024, issued a revenue forecast that fell short of analyst expectations, with projected revenue of $40.5 billion to $40.9 billion for fiscal year 2026 versus the $41.5 billion estimate. This tempered enthusiasm about AI agent returns, with CFO Dive reporting that Salesforce expects “modest” returns from its AI agent push this year.

Company Rollouts

Enterprises are deploying AI agents across diverse sectors, with concrete results emerging in healthcare, financial services, customer service, and logistics.

Healthcare

Innovaccer launched a suite of AI agents called “Agents of Care” designed to automate repetitive administrative tasks that contribute to clinician burnout. The agents handle scheduling, patient intake, referrals, and 24-hour support for patient inquiries. One agent conducts voice-activated protocol intake calls, asking patients questions about their emergency room visit and scheduling follow-ups. A referral agent connects patients with specialists and manages appointment logistics.

The rollout comes amid a projected shortage of 100,000 healthcare workers by 2028, according to consulting firm Mercer. Clinicians spend nearly nine hours per week on documentation alone, according to a Google Cloud study. Innovaccer, which recently raised $275 million in funding from investors including Generation Investment Management and Microsoft’s M12, is testing the agents at five health systems with general availability planned in two to three months.

Financial Services

BNY Mellon is managing “armies of AI agents” through its Eliza tool, an open-source system that enables multi-agent negotiations. The bank, America’s oldest, has deployed AI agents that can negotiate with each other to optimize internal processes. The system began development in 2023 and was released in 2024, with plans to upgrade to Eliza 2.0.

Goldman Sachs and Capital One are preparing for self-driving AI agents, according to American Banker. The financial institutions are exploring how agents can automate workflows while maintaining compliance in highly regulated environments. Routable added a fraud-detecting AI agent to its AP automation platform, identifying suspicious invoices and payment anomalies.

Customer Service

Cresta announced rapidly scaling AI voice agents in production, with strong results from deployments at Brinks Home Security. The AI Agent combines cutting-edge language models with business logic to deliver empathetic, human-like conversations that resolve complex issues. Brinks Home reported a 30-point increase in Net Promoter Score following the deployment.

Jotform launched AI Agents to transform customer service with a no-code solution. The platform enables organizations to deploy AI-powered virtual agents that manage inquiries and guide users through complex processes like booking, onboarding, and appointment scheduling. Jotform has over 30 million users worldwide .

HubSpot’s Agent.ai platform raced past 500,000 users after launching at INBOUND 2024. The platform, founded by HubSpot CTO Dharmesh Shah, grew from 250,000 users at the start of 2025, demonstrating rapid adoption. More than 5,000 people have used the low-code tool to build custom agents, and users have submitted 13,000 ratings and reviews with an average of 3.99 stars.

Real Estate

Christie’s is using AI agents to sell real estate and has generated $100 million in sales through the technology, according to Fox Business. The real estate giant’s Porta da Frente division has deployed agents to handle property transactions, demonstrating concrete ROI from AI agent adoption.

Telecom and Logistics

Deutsche Telekom partnered with Google Cloud on agentic AI for autonomous networks. The collaboration aims to develop AI agents that can manage network operations autonomously, improving efficiency and reducing manual intervention.

FourKites unveiled Tracy & Sam, two AI agents for supply chain efficiency. Tracy handles track and trace functions, automating repetitive tasks 24/7 and proactively contacting carriers to ensure data accuracy. Sam focuses on supplier collaboration, processing purchase orders and invoices. Early adopter Unilever reported improvements within four weeks of implementing Tracy, with the agent helping exception management and tracking quality. FourKites claims the Digital Workforce can increase shipment handling by 40% and automate up to 80% of routine tasks.

Sector Company Use Case Status
Healthcare Innovaccer Scheduling, patient intake, referrals Launched, testing at 5 systems
Financial Services BNY Mellon Managing agent fleets, multi-agent negotiations In production
Real Estate Christie’s Property sales $100M in sales
Customer Service Cresta Voice agents with Brinks Home Scaling in production
Customer Service HubSpot/Agent.ai Network of autonomous agents 500,000+ users
Telecom Deutsche Telekom Network operations with Google Cloud Pilot
Logistics FourKites Tracy & Sam efficiency agents Launched

Developer Tools & Infrastructure

A new distribution model is emerging: AI agent marketplaces. Cloud platforms are also making it easier to build agents, and developer tools are adding agent capabilities.

Marketplaces & Stores

Olas launched the first-ever AI agent store with $13.8 million in backing. The decentralized marketplace enables developers to publish and monetize AI agents, similar to app stores. The funding raised by Olas aims to accelerate the development of an ecosystem where agents can be discovered, composed, and deployed.

Enso launched an AI agent marketplace in partnership with LangChain. The platform offers pre-built agents for business tasks, enabling organizations to deploy AI automation without building from scratch.

Cloud Platforms

Microsoft Azure announced Azure AI Agent Service in public preview, available through AI Foundry SDK and Portal. The service enables developers to build secure, stateful, autonomous AI agents in code-first environments. Microsoft also unveiled GPT-4.5, the latest general-purpose model, alongside specialized models including Phi-4, Phi-4-Vision, Phi-4-Coding, and Phi-4-Audio. The Azure AI Foundry model library now exceeds 1,800 offerings .

Amazon Web Services (AWS) introduced Amazon Q Developer Agents, streamlining development with AI-powered coding assistance. AWS also published guidance on building agentic AI solutions with DeepSeek-R1, CrewAI, and Amazon SageMaker AI.

Google Cloud announced tools to build scalable AI agents with Langbase and the Gemini API. The platform enables developers to create agents that leverage Gemini 2.0 for complex reasoning tasks.

Snowflake launched AI agents powered by Anthropic’s Claude, integrating the large language model into its data cloud platform. The agents can analyze data and generate insights within Snowflake’s infrastructure.

Zoho Corporation announced Zia Agents, a platform supporting autonomous agents across its portfolio of 100+ products. Zia Agents, Agent Studio, and Agent Marketplace empower enterprises to access, build, and distribute intelligent digital agents. The company, which onboarded 110,000 new customers in 2024, is previewing pre-built, task-specific agents that will deploy across its combined portfolio.

Developer Tools

GitHub Copilot unveiled “The agent awakens,” adding agent capabilities to the development platform. The upgrade enables Copilot to handle more complex coding workflows autonomously.

Postman introduced AI Agent Builder with three key features: visual agent design, testing, and deployment. The tool helps developers create agents that interact with APIs.

Docker added agent capabilities for containerized applications, enabling AI-driven operations within its platform.

Infrastructure Considerations

The infrastructure stack for AI agents is evolving. The New Stack reported on why AI agents need an operational database , highlighting the need for databases that can handle the state management, transaction consistency, and real-time requirements of agentic workloads.

Cisco’s Outshift group predicted that average-size organizations will deploy 20,000 AI agents , with enterprises handling hundreds of thousands. This has sparked discussion of an “Internet of Agents”—an open, interoperable framework for agent-to-agent communication.

Research and Innovation

Research institutions and companies are exploring novel applications of AI agents, from robotics to chip design.

Microsoft Research introduced Magma, an AI foundation model that combines visual and language processing to control both software interfaces and robotic systems. Unlike prior systems requiring separate models for perception and control, Magma integrates these abilities. The model scored 80.0 on the VQAv2 benchmark , higher than GPT-4V’s 77.2, and achieved 87.4 on the POPE benchmark. Microsoft plans to release the code publicly on GitHub.

NVIDIA introduced Marco, a multi-AI agent framework for chip design. The configurable graph-based system enables multiple agents to collaborate on complex chip design tasks, representing a novel application of agentic AI in semiconductor engineering.

University of Oulu researchers developed MAI (metacognitive AI agent), an AI tutor that taught physics to 12-13-year-old students in Finland. Unlike traditional AI applications that provide ready-made answers, MAI supports independent problem-solving by prompting students to think. The pilot found that students “appreciated MAI’s prompting feature” and that the agent helped group work dynamics.

Napkin AI launched a ‘design agency’ of AI agents that generates professional graphics from text prompts in under five seconds. The company doubled its user base to 2 million in six weeks. The platform uses a team of specialized AI agents—an orchestrator LLM assigns tasks to styling, rendering, and layout agents—demonstrating a vertical approach to agentic AI.

Logie AI launched “Influencer’s Agent Army” for affiliate marketing, automating influencer campaign management at scale.

Various researchers are exploring car-buying agents, AI agents that would handle vehicle research, pricing negotiation, and purchase. Computerworld reported on how an AI agent could help you buy your next car .

Microsoft published ExACT (Improving AI agents’ decision-making via test-time compute scaling), a research framework for enhancing agent performance through increased computational investment during task execution.

Challenges and Concerns

While AI agents are advancing rapidly, researchers and practitioners are raising important concerns about deployment, safety, and societal impact.

Researchers warned that fully autonomous AI agents “should not be deployed.” A paper reviewed in Process Excellence Network stated, “We find no clear benefit of fully autonomous AI agents, but many foreseeable harms from ceding full human control.” The researchers found that risks increase with system autonomy, particularly safety risks that affect human life. They recommended adoption of agent levels, human control mechanisms, and safety verification.

A Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon University study found that some workers risk becoming overly reliant on generative AI, with problem-solving skills declining as a result. The survey of 319 knowledge workers collected 936 examples of AI use, finding that higher confidence in AI correlates with less critical thinking.

Job displacement concerns are emerging. Microsoft executive Georg Glantschnig told CFO Dive that some finance jobs may “disappear” as AI agents automate labor-intensive processes like financial close. However, he noted that new roles like “agent business administrators” are emerging.

Security risks are multiplying. Malwarebytes reported on new AI agents that could hold people for ransom, representing an evolution of ransomware threats.

Business model questions persist. Reuters Breakingviews analysis noted that AI agents have a clear mission but hazy business models. Investors see vast potential—Ark Investments estimates AI agents could enable $9 trillion of global e-commerce sales by 2030—but monetization paths remain uncertain.

Confusion about what agents actually are persists. UC Today documented “AI Agent Confusion” , noting that the term ranges from simple chatbots to fully autonomous systems, making it difficult for enterprises to evaluate solutions.

UX concerns are growing. Built In identified three things needed before AI agents go mainstream: improved trust and transparency, better error handling, and seamless integration into existing workflows.

Privacy issues are emerging. SC Media outlined five privacy concerns around agentic AI, including data collection, surveillance, and the potential for agents to expose sensitive information.

Responsible AI is becoming a priority. IBM published “The Rise of Responsible AI Agents” , emphasizing the need for ethical development practices.

Legal perspectives are emerging. Above the Law published guidance for in-house counsel on agents versus agentic AI, highlighting legal considerations for enterprise adoption.

Implementation challenges are significant. A Constellation Research report noted that AI agents bring new consumption models to SaaS, asking whether this represents a “Goldilocks or headache” for enterprises managing software costs.

Funding and Startups

Startup activity and funding rounds reflect growing investor interest in AI agent infrastructure and applications.

Olas raised $13.8 million to launch its decentralized AI agent store, according to VentureBeat . The funding aims to build a marketplace where agents can be discovered, composed, and deployed.

Qeen.ai, an AI agents for e-commerce startup founded by Google and DeepMind alumni, raised a $10 million seed round . The company, which employs 50 people, offers autonomous agents for e-commerce automation.

Pinkfish emerged from stealth with a $7.6 million pre-seed round led by Norwest Venture Partners. The startup helps enterprises build AI agents through natural language processing, with more than 200 integrations including Salesforce and Zendesk. Customers include Ipsy, Elevate, and Talkdesk.

SoftBank and OpenAI partnered to push AGI and agents, according to Axios . The partnership aims to accelerate the development of artificial general intelligence with Japanese focus.

Nvidia’s revenue is surging from agentic AI demand. CEO Jensen Huang reported that Blackwell GPU architecture booked $11 billion in Q4 revenue, with data center revenues more than doubling. The company sees agentic AI as the next stage after generative AI, with “physical AI” like robots following after.

India accounts for 40% of AI agent deployments globally for Automation Anywhere, driven by global capability centers and large enterprises. The company reported two-fold growth in AI agent deals and an 80% success rate from proof-of-concept to production.

Looking Ahead

Three distinct trends emerge from February’s developments:

First, AI agents are moving from prototypes to production. OpenAI’s Operator and Google’s AI co-scientist represent productized agents available to users, not just research demonstrations. The focus is shifting from “what can agents do?” to “how do we deploy and manage them at scale?”

Second, enterprises are building agent management systems. Workday’s Agent System of Record, ServiceNow’s AI Agent Orchestrator, and SAP’s Joule represent infrastructure for treating AI agents as digital employees. This reflects the recognition that managing fleets of agents requires new categories of enterprise software.

Third, new distribution channels are emerging. Agent marketplaces from Olas and Enso represent a new model for discovering and deploying AI agents. This could accelerate adoption by making agents easier to find and integrate.

The corporate venturing community is actively investing. Global Corporate Venturing reported that companies are rushing to invest in AI agent startups, sensing both opportunity and competitive threat.

Looking at a 10-year horizon, NFX predicted the rise of an “AI agent economy” , where agent marketplaces become the primary distribution channel for software and services.

However, expectations are outpacing reality. IBM’s analysis of “AI Agents in 2025: Expectations vs. Reality” noted that while excitement is high, many deployments remain in pilot or experimentation phases. Salesforce’s tempered revenue forecast reinforces that AI agent adoption will be gradual rather than explosive.

The workplace of the future will include both humans and AI agents. As Axios noted , workplace chat will feature more AI agents and fewer humans over time. The question is not whether AI agents will enter the workforce, but how quickly enterprises will adapt their management practices, security protocols, and workforce strategies to accommodate them.

2025 is shaping up to be the year of enterprise experimentation with AI agents—testing use cases, building management infrastructure, and learning what works. The transition to widespread production deployments will take longer, but the foundation is being laid now.
